title: The 4 Disciplines of Execution
author: Chris McChesney, Sean Covey, and Jim Huling
blurb: Most leaders can set a strategy. Far fewer can get it done. This book argues that the real enemy of execution is not laziness or bad ideas but the whirlwind, the endless urgent work that keeps the day running and swallows everything new. To break through, the authors offer four disciplines. First, focus on one or two wildly important goals instead of many. Second, act on lead measures, the small actions you control that drive results, rather than obsessing over lagging outcomes. Third, keep a simple, compelling scoreboard so the team always knows whether it is winning. Fourth, create a cadence of accountability through short weekly meetings where everyone commits to specific actions. Together, these disciplines turn vague strategy into steady, visible progress, even while the whirlwind keeps blowing.

lessons.b: The biggest threat to any important goal is the whirlwind, the urgent daily work that consumes the time and energy needed for anything new.
issues: scene 7: The magnifying glass sits on top of the drowning-figure box. It covers the box's right edge and the water. Its handle ends right against the 'DROWNING IN URGENT WORK' label, so the group reads as cluttered and stacked. (fix: Move the magnifier to the right of the box, into the gap before the culprit pills, or shrink it. Keep at least 24px clearance from the box and the label.)

scene 1: The 'NEW GOAL' label inside the whiteboard is very small and pale grey on white. It is close to the 18px minimum and barely legible. (fix: Raise the label to at least 20px and use the muted grey-blue at full opacity so it reads clearly.)

lessons.t: The Four Disciplines at a Glance
lessons.b: Execution becomes reliable when teams practise four connected disciplines: focus, lead measures, a scoreboard, and regular accountability.
issues: scene 1: The indigo X is drawn directly over the checklist text. It hides letters in 'PICK YOUR FAVOURITE?', 'FOCUS', 'ENGAGEMENT' and 'ACCOUNTABILITY', and covers the amber checkmark, so the card is partly unreadable. (fix: Keep the X inside the checkbox column, or draw it at lower opacity behind the text. Alternatively, show the rejection as a strikethrough on each label plus a small 'X' badge at the card's corner, so all label text stays legible.)

lessons.b: Discipline 1 says the more goals you chase at once, the fewer you achieve, so pick one or two that truly matter most.

lessons.t: From X to Y by When
lessons.b: A wildly important goal must be measurable and time-bound, written as moving from a starting line to a finish line by a deadline.
issues: scene 0: The two road edge lines are drawn on top of the fog clouds and cut through them, so the 'no finish line, lost in fog' drawing looks layered wrong. (fix: Put the cloud group above the road lines in z-order, or end the road lines at the cloud's lower edge, so the road fades into the fog.)

lessons.b: Discipline 2 says to track the predictive actions you can influence, like daily calories and exercise, rather than only the end result, like weight lost.
issues: scene 3: The dessert icon is hard to read. The cake slice is drawn as a cramped wedge with a diagonal strike through it, and a checkmark sits against its left edge. Showing a check and a cross-out on the same object sends a mixed signal and makes the drawing look broken. (fix: Redraw the cake slice as a clear, simple wedge with a cherry, then show 'skip' one way only: either a single strike or a 'no' circle over the cake. Move the checkmark so it has clear space and does not touch the cake.)

lessons.b: Discipline 3 says a simple, visible scoreboard showing whether the team is winning drives far more engagement than a complex report.
Discipline 4 says short, regular team sessions, where people report on last week's commitments and make new ones, keep the goal alive.
issues: scene 8: The closing scene is mostly text. A small notepad icon sits in the top-right corner, and much of the right half and bottom of the stage is empty. Nothing pictures the action of scheduling a weekly 20-minute check or each person naming one action. (fix: Add a supporting visual on the right, such as a calendar with one day and time circled and a small 20-minute timer, or a row of team figures each holding a single action card. Rebalance the text block so the stage is filled.)

lessons.b: The four disciplines work together to protect a small slice of time for your top goal, so progress happens even while the whirlwind keeps blowing.
issues: scene 7: The 'NEW' label inside the small amber dot is tiny, roughly 16px at 1600 width. The dot also sits almost touching the neighbouring navy dot, so the pair reads as cramped. (fix: Enlarge the NEW circle to about 60px diameter with at least 18px text. Move it inward, away from the adjacent dot, so there is clear spacing.)

scene 4: The amber dashed attention lines from the people's heads run straight through several floating whirlwind cards. The lines and card outlines overlap and look tangled. (fix: Reposition the floating cards higher or further left, away from the line paths. Alternatively, draw the lines beneath the cards with a stage-coloured gap so they don't visually collide.)

scene 8: The 'BLOCKED' label floats far to the upper right of the clock, detached from the amber wedge it describes. The wedge also overlaps the 12 o'clock tick mark. (fix: Place 'BLOCKED' directly beside the wedge's outer edge, or add a short leader line to it. Draw the tick marks above the wedge, or trim the wedge so the 12 o'clock tick stays visible.)
